features.description: Second-person plural pronoun or address form.
features.safe_example: Y'all can see why the character returns.
features.blocked_context: Do not insert when no second-person reference exists.

features.description: Expanded second-person plural form, often used for a whole group.
features.safe_example: All y'all can see the main reason.
features.blocked_context: Use only for plural addressee contexts.

features.description: Near-future quasi-modal roughly meaning about to.
features.safe_example: She is fixin' to try again.
features.blocked_context: Do not use unless the anchor expresses an upcoming action.

features.description: Regional verb meaning think or suppose.
features.safe_example: I reckon the author wanted to show hope.

features.description: Regional intensifier in expressions such as right hard/right much.
features.blocked_context: Use sparingly and avoid comic tone.

features.description: Regional expression with context-dependent pragmatic meaning.
features.blocked_context: Avoid in benchmark generation unless the team explicitly approves the pragmatic context.
Do not use if completion is not part of the original meaning.

features.description: Stacked modal construction such as might could.
features.safe_example: She might could take the test again.
features.blocked_context: Do not add uncertainty if the anchor states certainty.

features.description: Coreferential pronoun after a verb, often highlighting subject involvement.
features.safe_example: I wrote me a short answer.
features.blocked_context: Use only when the subject is intentionally involved and a direct object is present.

features.description: Prefix a- attaches to compatible progressive -ing verb forms.
features.safe_example: He kept a-trying after he failed.
features.blocked_context: Use only with compatible progressive verbs; avoid noun/adjective -ing forms.

features.description: Nonstandard negative auxiliary form listed in the paper appendix as orthographic material.
features.blocked_context: Use only where a negative auxiliary already exists; avoid caricature or added negation.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: One after a disjunction to mean one or the other.
features.safe_example: He had to choose reading or writing, one.
features.blocked_context: Use only when an either/or contrast already exists.

features.description: Wh-word followed by all to ask about a set of items or places.
features.safe_example: What all did the student explain?
features.blocked_context: Use only in question-like contexts; avoid changing declarative answers into questions.

features.description: Use of anymore in non-negative contexts.
features.safe_example: People use computers for many things anymore.
features.blocked_context: Use only when it does not change time/aspect meaning.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.blocked_context: Avoid phonetic spelling unless team approves an orthographic perturbation condition.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

safety_notes: Do not make the student sound less intelligent or less educated.
Prefer grammatical and lexical features that preserve the exact proposition.
